why.correct: The occipital lobe is the back of each hemisphere, behind the parieto-occipital sulcus and above the cerebellum. It handles vision.
options: The parietal lobe lies on top, between the central sulcus and the parieto-occipital sulcus, in front of the pinned lobe.
The temporal lobe lies along the side below the lateral sulcus, not at the back of the hemisphere.
Correct. The rearmost lobe, sitting above the cerebellum, is the occipital lobe.
The frontal lobe is at the front of the hemisphere, in front of the central sulcus.

why.correct: The central sulcus runs from the top of the hemisphere down its side and separates the frontal lobe in front from the parietal lobe behind.
options: The lateral sulcus is the deep groove along the side of the brain with the temporal lobe below it; it runs front to back, not over the top.
Correct. The groove between the frontal and parietal lobes is the central sulcus.
The parieto-occipital sulcus lies further back, between the parietal and occipital lobes.
The longitudinal fissure runs front to back down the midline between the two hemispheres, so a side view does not show it as a groove across the hemisphere.

why.correct: The pons is the rounded bulge in the middle of the brainstem, between the midbrain above and the medulla below. Its bulk is axons crossing to the cerebellum.
options: The midbrain is the short top part of the brainstem, above the pinned bulge.
The medulla oblongata is the narrow lowest part that continues as the spinal cord, below the pinned bulge.
The cerebellum lies behind the brainstem; it is not part of the brainstem itself.
Correct. The bulging middle part of the brainstem is the pons.

why.correct: The hypothalamus lies below and in front of the thalamus, with the pituitary gland hanging from its underside. It is part of the diencephalon.
options: Correct. The region below the thalamus that the pituitary hangs from is the hypothalamus.
The thalamus is the larger, egg-shaped mass above and behind the pinned region.
The pituitary gland hangs below on a short stalk; the pinned region is the part of the brain it hangs from.
The midbrain is the top of the brainstem, behind and below the pinned region.

why.correct: The longitudinal fissure is the deep midline groove that separates the right and left cerebral hemispheres.
options: The central sulcus runs across each hemisphere from top to side, separating frontal from parietal lobe; it does not divide the two hemispheres.
The corpus callosum is the band of white matter at the floor of this groove, deep inside, not the groove itself.
Correct. The midline groove between the hemispheres is the longitudinal fissure.
The lateral sulcus is on the side of each hemisphere, above the temporal lobe.

why.correct: The hippocampus curls along the floor of the temporal lobe at the bottom of the limbic ring. It is needed to form new memories of facts and events.
options: The amygdala is the small almond-shaped mass at the front tip of the hippocampus, not the long curved structure.
Correct. The curved structure along the bottom of the limbic ring is the hippocampus.
The cingulate gyrus arches over the top of the corpus callosum, at the top of the ring.
The corpus callosum is the white-matter band in the middle of the ring, joining the two hemispheres.

why.correct: The putamen is the outermost of the basal nuclei in this section. With the caudate it forms the striatum.
options: The caudate lies closer to the midline, beside the central fluid space, not in the outer position.
The globus pallidus lies just inside the putamen, toward the midline.
The thalamus is part of the diencephalon, lower and nearer the midline; this slice is taken in front of it.
Correct. The outer mass is the putamen.

why.correct: The hindbrain (rhombencephalon) splits into the metencephalon, which becomes the pons and cerebellum, and the myelencephalon, which becomes the medulla oblongata.
options: The myelencephalon is the lower half of the hindbrain; it becomes the medulla oblongata.
The mesencephalon does not split and becomes the midbrain.
Correct. The metencephalon forms the pons and the cerebellum.
The telencephalon becomes the cerebrum.

why.correct: Neurulation turns the flat neural plate into the neural tube by the end of the fourth week. Its front end then swells into three primary vesicles, and by the fifth week the forebrain and hindbrain have split to give five.
options: The neural plate is the starting point, in the third week.
The plate folds up at its edges, leaving a groove down the middle.
Fusion of the folds closes the tube; this ends neurulation.
The three primary vesicles are the forebrain, midbrain and hindbrain.
The five secondary vesicles become the adult brain regions.

why.correct: Clumsy, poorly timed movement with normal strength is ataxia, the sign of cerebellar damage. Each side of the cerebellum coordinates the same side of the body, so a clumsy left hand points to the left cerebellum.
options: Correct. Ataxia of the left arm comes from the left side of the cerebellum.
The cerebellum coordinates the same side, not the opposite side, so right-sided damage would make the right hand clumsy.
Damage to the frontal lobe's movement areas causes weakness on the opposite side. Mr. Brandt's strength is normal, and his left side is affected.
The occipital lobe handles vision; damage there causes loss of vision in part of what you see, not clumsy reaching with normal sight.

why.correct: These are the signs of Parkinson's disease. Dopamine from the substantia nigra makes it easier for the striatum to release the brake on a planned movement. When those neurons die, the brake stays on too hard, so movement is slow and hard to start, muscles are stiff, and a tremor appears at rest.
options: Loss of hippocampal neurons impairs forming new memories, not starting movements.
Correct. Death of dopamine neurons in the substantia nigra causes Parkinson's disease.
Cerebellar damage causes ataxia: movement that overshoots and staggers, with a tremor during movement rather than at rest, and no difficulty starting.
Loss of the reticular activating system lowers alertness and can cause coma; it does not cause a resting tremor.

why.correct: The reticular activating system, in the core of the brainstem, sends a steady stream of signals through the thalamus that keeps the cortex awake. Destroy it on both sides and even an undamaged cortex cannot be roused, which is coma.
options: The basal nuclei lie deep in the cerebrum, not in the brainstem, and their loss affects the selection of movement, not wakefulness.
The corpus callosum lies in the cerebrum. Cutting it leaves a person fully awake; the hemispheres just share less information.
The hypothalamus is in the diencephalon, not the brainstem core, and loss of temperature control does not by itself prevent waking.
Correct. Loss of the reticular activating system on both sides causes coma.

why.correct: The hypothalamus is the control center for temperature, water balance and thirst, hunger, autonomic output and the pituitary gland. Correcting movement is the cerebellum's job, and relaying touch to the cortex is the thalamus's.
options: Yes. Hypothalamic neurons sense blood temperature and drive sweating, skin blood flow and shivering.
Yes. The hypothalamus creates thirst and controls a hormone that makes the kidneys keep water.
Yes. The hypothalamus controls the pituitary gland just below it.
No. Correcting the force and timing of movement is the cerebellum's job.
Yes. The hypothalamus sends axons to the brainstem and spinal cord neurons of the sympathetic and parasympathetic divisions.
No. Relaying touch and other body sensations to the cortex is the thalamus's job.

why.correct: Losing substantia nigra dopamine leaves the basal nuclei's brake on movement on too hard: the thalamus stays inhibited and movement is slow and hard to start. Memory formation, a hippocampal job, is not directly affected.

variables.name: Dopamine released into the striatum
variables.why: The substantia nigra is the source of the striatum's dopamine, so fewer neurons release less of it.

variables.name: Ease of starting a planned movement
variables.why: Dopamine makes it easier for the striatum to release the globus pallidus's brake on the thalamus; with less dopamine the brake stays on, so movements are hard to start.

variables.name: Inhibition of the thalamus by the globus pallidus
variables.why: Without dopamine's help, the striatum cannot switch off the globus pallidus's output as well, so the thalamus stays more inhibited.

variables.name: Ability to form new memories of events
variables.why: New memories of events depend on the hippocampus, which this loss does not directly affect.

why.correct: The basal nuclei loop runs cortex → striatum → globus pallidus → thalamus → cortex. The globus pallidus sends its output to the thalamus, not to the cerebellum.
options: Right. The striatum receives the input to the basal nuclei from the cortex.
Right. The striatum acts on the globus pallidus, the output nucleus.
This is the error. The globus pallidus inhibits the thalamus, which relays back to the cortex; the cerebellum runs a separate correcting loop.
Right. Through the thalamus, the loop returns to the cortex's motor areas.

why.correct: The diencephalon (thalamus, hypothalamus, epithalamus) sits between the cerebrum above and the brainstem, which starts with the midbrain, below.
options: Correct. The diencephalon links the cerebrum to the brainstem.
The cerebellum lies behind the brainstem, attached beside the pons, not in the line from cerebrum to midbrain.
The corpus callosum is white matter inside the cerebrum, joining the two hemispheres side to side.
The basal nuclei are gray matter inside the cerebrum, not a separate level below it.

why.correct: The lowest part of the brainstem is the medulla oblongata, which passes through the foramen magnum. Its nuclei set the basic rhythm of breathing, the heartbeat and blood vessel diameter, so crushing it stops breathing and circulation.
options: Smell does not depend on the medulla, and losing it is not life-threatening.
Correct. Compressing the medulla stops breathing and circulation.
Forming new memories depends on the hippocampus in the temporal lobe, not the medulla.
Coordination depends on the cerebellum. It may be affected too, but losing it is not what kills first.

why.correct: Smell signals reach the cortex, and the limbic system, without first relaying in the thalamus. Every other sense passes through the thalamus first.
options: Visual signals relay in the thalamus before reaching the occipital lobe.
Correct. Smell is the one sense that bypasses the thalamus on its way to the cortex.
Hearing signals relay in the thalamus before reaching the temporal lobe.
Touch signals from the body relay in the thalamus before reaching the parietal lobe.

why.correct: The internal capsule is the compact band that carries the axons running between the cortex and the brainstem and spinal cord. Movement commands for the left side of the body come from the right hemisphere, so damage to the right internal capsule weakens the left side.
options: Clumsy staggering movement with normal strength is cerebellar ataxia, and the right side of the body is controlled by the left hemisphere.
Smell does not travel through the internal capsule.
Correct. Motor axons from the right hemisphere pass through the right internal capsule and control the left side.
Each ear sends signals to both sides of the brain, and hearing does not depend on this band.

why.correct: In the strict terms of the nervous system, a nucleus is a cluster of neuron cell bodies inside the CNS and a ganglion is one outside it. These structures are deep in the cerebrum, so they are nuclei. "Basal ganglia" is the older name, still common.
options: They are gray matter, masses of cell bodies, not white matter.
They lie deep in the cerebrum, not the brainstem.
They are made of neurons, with glia among them like all gray matter.
Correct. Inside the CNS a cluster of cell bodies is a nucleus.

why.correct: The amygdala judges how emotionally important something is, especially a threat, and drives fear and its body responses through the hypothalamus. Without both amygdalae, fear responses are blunted.
options: Vision depends on the occipital lobe, not the amygdala.
Unsteady walking and slurred speech are signs of cerebellar damage.
Correct. Losing the amygdalae blunts fear.
Temperature control is the hypothalamus's job.

why.correct: The insula is a buried island of cortex at the bottom of the lateral sulcus. You see it only when you pull the temporal lobe down.
options: That describes the cingulate gyrus, part of the limbic lobe.
That describes the cerebellum.
That describes the hypothalamus.
Correct. The insula is hidden in the lateral sulcus.

why.correct: The dura mater is the thick outer meningeal layer against the inside of the skull. In the skull it has two layers, which split to enclose the venous channel in the midline.
options: Correct. The thick layer against the bone is the dura mater.
The arachnoid mater is the thin layer just inside the dura, with web-like strands reaching down to the pia.
The pia mater is the thin layer stuck to the brain surface, following it into the sulci.
The web-like strands cross the subarachnoid space below the arachnoid; the pinned layer is the thick sheet against the bone.

why.correct: The subarachnoid space lies between the arachnoid and the pia. It is a real space, crossed by web-like strands and filled with CSF.
options: The subdural space lies between the dura and the arachnoid, above the pinned space, and is normally only a potential space.
Correct. The space crossed by strands between the arachnoid and the pia is the subarachnoid space.
The epidural space lies outside the dura, between it and the bone; in the skull it is only a potential space.
The longitudinal fissure is the deep groove between the two hemispheres, not a space between meningeal layers.

why.correct: The choroid plexus is a tuft of capillaries covered by modified ependymal cells inside each ventricle. It secretes most of the CSF.
options: Arachnoid granulations sit at the top of the head, where CSF returns to venous blood, not inside a ventricle.
The interventricular foramen is the small opening from each lateral ventricle into the third ventricle, not a tuft of tissue.
Correct. The tuft of tissue in the ventricle is the choroid plexus.
The corpus callosum is the white-matter band above the lateral ventricles, not a source of fluid.

why.correct: The cerebral aqueduct is the narrow canal through the midbrain that joins the third ventricle to the fourth.
options: The central canal runs down the middle of the spinal cord, below the fourth ventricle.
Correct. The canal through the midbrain is the cerebral aqueduct.
The interventricular foramen joins each lateral ventricle to the third ventricle, higher up in the brain.
The median aperture is an opening in the roof of the fourth ventricle into the subarachnoid space.

why.correct: The fourth ventricle is the tent-shaped space between the pons and medulla in front and the cerebellum behind.
options: The third ventricle is a narrow midline slit in the diencephalon, higher up.
The lateral ventricles lie deep in the cerebral hemispheres.
The subarachnoid space surrounds the brain outside the pia; the pinned space is inside the brain.
Correct. The chamber between brainstem and cerebellum is the fourth ventricle.

why.correct: CSF made in the lateral ventricles passes through the interventricular foramina to the third ventricle, down the cerebral aqueduct to the fourth ventricle, out through the apertures into the subarachnoid space, and back into venous blood at the arachnoid granulations.
options: The choroid plexuses of the lateral ventricles make the most CSF, which drains through the interventricular foramina.
The third ventricle lies in the midline of the diencephalon.
The aqueduct runs through the midbrain.
The fourth ventricle lies between the brainstem and the cerebellum; CSF leaves it through the median and lateral apertures.
CSF spreads around the brain and spinal cord here.
The granulations push into the venous channels in the dura, where CSF enters the blood.

why.correct: The cerebral aqueduct, running through the midbrain, carries CSF from the third ventricle to the fourth.
options: Correct. The aqueduct links the third and fourth ventricles.
The central canal continues below the fourth ventricle into the spinal cord.
The median aperture is an exit from the fourth ventricle, after it, not before it.
Arachnoid granulations are where CSF leaves the subarachnoid space, at the end of the path.

why.correct: CSF flows one way: lateral ventricles → third ventricle → cerebral aqueduct → fourth ventricle → apertures. It does not flow back up from the fourth ventricle into the lateral ventricles; it leaves the fourth ventricle through the apertures.
options: Right. The lateral ventricles' choroid plexuses make most of the CSF.
Right. The interventricular foramina join the lateral ventricles to the third.
This is the error. From the fourth ventricle, CSF flows out into the subarachnoid space, not back up.
Right. The apertures are the exits into the subarachnoid space.

why.correct: A block at the cerebral aqueduct traps CSF made in the lateral and third ventricles. Those ventricles swell and pressure in the skull rises, while the fourth ventricle below the block stays normal and secretion continues: obstructive hydrocephalus.

variables.name: Size of the lateral ventricles
variables.why: The choroid plexuses above the block keep secreting CSF, which cannot pass the aqueduct, so it builds up and swells the ventricles above it.

variables.name: Size of the fourth ventricle
variables.why: The fourth ventricle lies below the block. Its own CSF still drains out through the apertures, so it stays normal size.

variables.name: Pressure inside the skull
variables.why: Fluid is added to a closed bony box faster than it leaves, so the swelling ventricles press the brain against the skull and pressure rises.

variables.name: Rate of CSF secretion by the choroid plexuses
variables.why: Secretion is driven by the choroid plexus cells' ion pumping and changes little as pressure rises, which is why the fluid keeps building up.

why.correct: A blow to the thin temporal bone can tear the middle meningeal artery, which runs on the inside of the skull. Its arterial blood peels the dura off the bone, making a compact, lens-shaped epidural hematoma that stops at the sutures, where the dura is most firmly attached. Arterial pressure makes it grow fast.
options: Torn bridging veins cause a subdural hematoma, which spreads as a thin crescent and usually builds more slowly.
A burst artery at the base of the brain bleeds into the subarachnoid space, mixing blood with CSF rather than forming a lens-shaped clot against the skull.
The choroid plexus lies inside the ventricles, far from the skull, and does not cause a clot between skull and dura.
Correct. A torn middle meningeal artery causes an epidural hematoma.

why.correct: This is a chronic subdural hematoma: blood from torn bridging veins between the dura and the arachnoid. Nothing holds those layers together, so blood spreads as a crescent. Brain shrinkage with age stretches the bridging veins, the blood thinner keeps them bleeding, and low venous pressure makes it build slowly.
options: Blood between skull and dura is an epidural hematoma, which is usually arterial, fast and lens-shaped.
Blood in the subarachnoid space mixes with the CSF and outlines the sulci; it usually causes a sudden severe headache.
Correct. A slowly building crescent over the brain is a subdural hematoma.
Blood inside a ventricle would sit in the fluid spaces deep in the brain, not over the surface of a hemisphere.

why.correct: A lumbar puncture samples fluid from the subarachnoid space. Blood in that fluid means blood entered the subarachnoid space and mixed with the CSF: a subarachnoid hemorrhage, typically from a burst weak spot in an artery at the base of the brain.
options: Correct. Blood in the CSF places the bleed in the subarachnoid space.
Blood in the epidural space collects outside the dura and does not mix with the CSF that a lumbar puncture samples.
Blood in the subdural space lies outside the arachnoid and does not enter the CSF.
The choroid plexus makes CSF, but a sudden worst-ever headache with bloody CSF points to a burst artery in the subarachnoid space.

why.correct: The pia mater is a very thin layer attached to the brain's surface, dipping into every sulcus and carrying small blood vessels.
options: Correct. The pia mater follows the brain surface everywhere.
The dura mater is the tough outer layer against the skull.
The arachnoid mater lies against the dura and bridges over the sulci rather than following them.
The inner layer of the dura faces the brain but only folds down between major parts, such as the hemispheres, not into each sulcus.

why.correct: Brain capillary endothelial cells are sealed by tight junctions, so substances must pass through the cells. Small lipid-soluble molecules dissolve straight through the cell membranes, so an anesthetic gas crosses easily.
options: Large proteins cannot pass between the sealed cells, and brain endothelium carries very few transport vesicles, so they barely enter.
Dopamine is water-soluble and has no carrier protein in the barrier, so it stays in the blood. Its precursor levodopa, an amino acid, is carried across instead.
Correct. Small lipid-soluble molecules cross the barrier freely.
Charged ions cannot dissolve through the lipid membrane and cannot slip between the sealed cells, so they cross only slowly through specific channels and pumps.

why.correct: The barrier is the brain capillary endothelium: cells sealed edge to edge by tight junctions, with no pores and few vesicles. Everything entering brain tissue has to pass through these cells.
options: Astrocyte end-feet cover the capillaries and keep the endothelium in its barrier state, but molecules could slip between them; they are not the barrier itself.
The pia mater is a meningeal layer on the brain's surface, not part of every capillary wall.
Correct. The sealed endothelial cells are the barrier.
The choroid plexus covering cells form the blood–CSF barrier, a separate barrier between blood and CSF.

why.correct: In an adult the spinal cord ends at about the first or second lumbar vertebra, but the CSF-filled subarachnoid space continues to about the second sacral vertebra. Below the cord's end, the needle meets only floating nerve roots, which slide away from it.
options: The reason is not the width of the space in the neck; it is that the lower back holds no spinal cord to injure.
Correct. Below the end of the cord, the needle cannot hit the cord.
The dura continues to about the second sacral vertebra, and the needle must pass through it to reach the CSF.
There is no choroid plexus in the spinal canal; CSF there has flowed down from the brain.

why.correct: The choroid plexus cells are joined by tight junctions and secrete CSF rather than letting plasma leak through, so CSF has almost no protein, very few cells, and glucose about two thirds of the blood level.
options: Yes. CSF protein is less than 1% of the plasma level.
Yes. Normal CSF has only a few white blood cells and no red cells.
Yes. CSF glucose is about two thirds of the blood level.
No. CSF has much less protein than plasma, not more.
No. Red blood cells in CSF mean bleeding into the subarachnoid space, or a needle that nicked a vessel.

why.correct: The subarachnoid space, between the arachnoid and the pia, is a real space filled with CSF. The epidural and subdural spaces in the skull open only when something such as blood forces the layers apart.
options: In the skull the dura is fused to the bone, so the epidural space is only a potential space. Around the spinal cord it is real.
The arachnoid lies pressed against the dura, so the subdural space is only a potential space.
The dura's two layers are fused except where they split to enclose the venous channels; there is no general fluid space between them.
Correct. The subarachnoid space is real and holds CSF.

why.correct: In an infant the skull bones are separated by soft gaps, so as CSF builds up the skull expands and the head grows. In an adult the fused skull cannot expand, so the same build-up raises pressure inside the skull, which causes headache, vomiting and drowsiness.
options: Adults do get hydrocephalus; when the path is blocked or the granulations are clogged, fluid builds up whatever their age.
Correct. An unfused skull expands; a fused one cannot, so pressure rises.
Adults do have arachnoid granulations; the difference lies in whether the skull can expand.
An infant's ventricles do swell with the extra fluid; the difference lies in whether the skull around them can grow.

why.correct: Ventricles above a block enlarge and those below stay normal. The third ventricle is enlarged and the fourth is not, so the block lies between them: the cerebral aqueduct.
options: A failure of return at the arachnoid granulations would back fluid up into all four ventricles, including the fourth.
A block at the apertures would enlarge the fourth ventricle too, since it lies above them.
A block at one interventricular foramen would enlarge only that lateral ventricle, not the third ventricle.
Correct. A block in the cerebral aqueduct enlarges the lateral and third ventricles and spares the fourth.

why.correct: A few small areas around the ventricles have leaky capillaries, so their neurons can sample the blood directly. One on the floor of the fourth ventricle detects toxins and triggers vomiting.
options: Correct. This area lacks the barrier, so its neurons sense the toxin in the blood.
Tight junctions seal the gaps between cells; molecules do not dissolve through them.
CSF flows from the brain down to the lumbar region and back up around the cord slowly; a toxin that cannot cross into CSF would not be in it in the first place.
Astrocyte end-feet do not ferry molecules across the capillary wall; they keep the endothelium sealed.

why.correct: Pointer 7 marks the broad gray horn reaching toward the front: the ventral (anterior) horn, which holds the cell bodies of motor neurons to skeletal muscle.
options: The dorsal horn is the narrow gray horn reaching toward the back, at pointer 3.
The lateral horn is the small gray bump at the side, at pointer 4.
The anterior column is white matter at the front beside the midline, at pointer 8, not gray matter.
Correct. The broad front horn of gray matter is the ventral horn.

why.correct: Pointer 11 marks the swelling on the root entering the back of the cord: the dorsal root ganglion, which holds the cell bodies of sensory neurons.
options: Correct. The swelling on the dorsal root is the dorsal root ganglion.
The ventral root leaves the front of the cord, at pointer 12, and has no swelling.
The lateral column is white matter inside the cord, at pointer 5.
The central canal is the tiny hole in the center of the cord, at pointer 6.

why.correct: Pointer 9 marks the deep, wide groove in the midline at the front of the cord: the anterior median fissure.
options: The posterior median sulcus is the shallow groove at the back, at pointer 1.
Correct. The deep front groove is the anterior median fissure.
The central canal is the tiny hole in the center, at pointer 6.
The anterior column is the white matter beside the fissure, at pointer 8, not the groove itself.

why.correct: The lateral horn, the small gray bump at the side (pointer 4), holds sympathetic motor neurons. It is present only in the thoracic and upper lumbar segments, T1 to L2.
options: Pointer 3 is the dorsal horn, which is sensory and present at every level.
Pointer 7 is the ventral horn, which holds somatic motor neurons to skeletal muscle; it is largest in the enlargements but present at every level.
Correct. The lateral horn holds sympathetic neurons, from T1 to L2.
Pointer 11 is the dorsal root ganglion, which holds sensory cell bodies at every level.

why.correct: Pointer 2 marks the white matter between the dorsal horn and the posterior median sulcus: the posterior column, made almost entirely of ascending tracts.
options: The dorsal horn is the gray matter beside it, at pointer 3.
The lateral column is the white matter at the side, between the dorsal and ventral horns, at pointer 5.
Correct. The white matter between the dorsal horn and the midline at the back is the posterior column.
The posterior median sulcus is the shallow groove in the midline at the back, at pointer 1.

why.correct: In an adult the cord tapers to the conus medullaris at about L1–L2, because the vertebral column grew longer than the cord.
options: Correct. The conus medullaris lies at about L1–L2.
The cord runs well below the neck, through the whole thoracic region.
The cord reaches a little lower than T12, into the upper lumbar region.
S2 is where the dural sac and subarachnoid space end, not the cord.

why.correct: The cauda equina (horse's tail) is the bundle of long lumbar and sacral roots running down the vertebral canal below the end of the cord, on their way to their exit holes.
options: The cone-shaped end of the cord is the conus medullaris; the cauda equina hangs below it.
Correct. The cauda equina is roots, not cord.
The widened part supplying the lower limbs is the lumbar enlargement.
That strand of pia anchors the cord below; the cauda equina is the bundle of roots hanging around it.

why.correct: At L4–L5 the vertebral canal holds no spinal cord, only the cauda equina: the lumbar and sacral roots on their way down. Crushing them causes leg weakness, numbness of the saddle area and loss of bladder control, a surgical emergency.
options: The conus medullaris lies at about L1–L2, above the burst disc.
The cervical enlargement is in the neck and supplies the upper limbs.
The lumbar enlargement is part of the cord and lies behind the lower thoracic vertebrae, well above L4–L5.
Correct. At L4–L5 the canal holds only the cauda equina.

why.correct: The cervical enlargement supplies the upper limbs, which have far more muscle and skin than a stretch of trunk. Its segments hold more motor neurons and receive more sensory axons, so they have more gray matter.
options: Correct. More neurons for the limbs means more gray matter and a wider cord.
The width is the cord's own tissue, not its coverings.
The central canal is tiny everywhere and often partly closed in adults.
The cord does not swell to fill the space; its width reflects how many neurons it holds.

why.correct: Dorsal roots carry sensory axons into the cord; ventral roots carry motor axons out. With the middle root and both its neighbors cut, no sensory route from that band reaches the cord, while the motor axons in the intact ventral roots still drive the muscles. Cutting one dorsal root alone would only dull the feeling, because neighboring roots overlap.
options: Paralysis with normal sensation would follow cutting the ventral roots, which carry the motor axons.
Correct. Cutting the dorsal roots removes sensation and spares strength.
Losing both would need both roots cut, or the nerve beyond where they join.
The ventral roots carry motor axons out; sensory signals enter through the dorsal roots.

why.correct: Ventral horn motor neurons are the only route from the cord to the skeletal muscles they supply. Destroying those in the lumbar enlargement weakens and wastes the leg muscles, while sensation (dorsal side) and the arms (cervical enlargement) are spared.

variables.name: Strength of the leg muscles
variables.why: The lumbar enlargement's ventral horns hold the motor neurons for the legs. With them gone, fewer commands reach the leg muscles, so they weaken.

variables.name: Sensation from the skin of the legs
variables.why: Sensation enters through the dorsal roots and dorsal horns, which the virus spared, so touch and pain from the legs still reach the brain.

variables.name: Size of the leg muscles
variables.why: Muscles that no longer receive signals from their motor neurons waste away over weeks.

variables.name: Strength of the arm muscles
variables.why: The arm muscles are supplied from the cervical enlargement, which the virus did not reach.

why.correct: The dorsal root brings sensory axons into the back of the cord. Their cell bodies sit outside the cord in the dorsal root ganglion, and the neurons are pseudounipolar: one process runs to the body, the other into the cord.
options: Yes. The dorsal root is the sensory way in.
Yes. The dorsal root ganglion holds the sensory cell bodies.
No. Motor axons leave through the ventral root.
Yes. Dorsal root ganglion neurons are pseudounipolar.
No. Ventral horn cell bodies send their axons out through the ventral root; dorsal root cell bodies sit in the ganglion.

why.correct: After chickenpox the virus lies dormant in the cell bodies of sensory neurons in a dorsal root ganglion. When it reactivates as shingles, it travels out along that ganglion's sensory axons, so the rash follows the band of skin that one dorsal root supplies, on one side only.
options: Ventral horn neurons are motor neurons; the rash follows a sensory territory.
Correct. The virus hides in a dorsal root ganglion.
Lateral horn neurons are sympathetic motor neurons, not the sensory neurons whose axons reach the skin.
The posterior column holds axons running up the cord, not the cell bodies where the virus waits.

why.correct: White matter thins going down the cord: fewer ascending axons have joined yet, and most descending axons have already left for their target segments. The thinnest white matter is at the sacral end, and lateral horns are absent below L2.
options: The upper cervical cord has the most white matter, since it carries every ascending and descending axon for the whole body.
Middle thoracic segments have lateral horns, which this section lacks.
Upper lumbar segments (to L2) still have lateral horns and more white matter than the sacral cord.
Correct. A thin white rim with no lateral horns fits the sacral cord.

why.correct: The sensory signal runs past its cell body in the dorsal root ganglion, enters through the dorsal root and reaches the dorsal horn. An interneuron passes it to a ventral horn motor neuron, whose axon leaves through the ventral root to the muscle.
options: The sensory neuron fires in the skin of the sole.
Its cell body sits in the dorsal root ganglion, beside the path of the signal.
The central process enters the cord through the dorsal root.
In the dorsal horn, the signal passes to an interneuron.
The interneuron excites a motor neuron in the ventral horn.
The motor axon leaves through the ventral root toward the leg muscle.

why.correct: Tract names give origin first and destination second. "Spino-" first means it starts in the spinal cord; the brain region second is where it ends. So it is ascending and carries sensory information up.
options: That would be a tract named brain region first and "-spinal" second.
A tract named for a brain region ends in that region, so it leaves the cord.
Correct. Origin first, destination second: this is an ascending tract.
Tracts run inside the CNS; axons leaving through the ventral roots belong to motor neurons, not to a tract.

why.correct: Motor neurons to skeletal muscle sit in the ventral (anterior) horn, not the dorsal horn. The dorsal horn is the sensory side, where many incoming sensory axons end.
options: Right. Motor commands travel down in descending tracts.
Right. Tracts run in the white columns.
This is the error. The motor neurons are in the ventral horn.
Right. Motor axons leave through the ventral root.

why.correct: Many sensory axons entering through the dorsal root end in the dorsal horn, on interneurons and on neurons that relay the signal up the cord.
options: Correct. Many incoming sensory axons end in the dorsal horn.
The ventral horn holds motor neurons, reached through interneurons, not directly by the dorsal root.
The lateral horn holds sympathetic motor neurons.
The ventral root carries motor axons out of the cord.

why.correct: The dorsal root ganglion sits on the dorsal root outside the spinal cord, so it is part of the peripheral nervous system. That is why its cluster of cell bodies is called a ganglion, not a nucleus.
options: The ventral horn is gray matter inside the spinal cord.
The posterior column is white matter inside the spinal cord.
The central canal runs through the middle of the spinal cord.
Correct. The dorsal root ganglion lies outside the cord.

why.correct: Early in fetal life the cord fills the whole canal. From then on the vertebral column grows faster and longer than the cord, so the cord's end sits relatively higher with age: about L3 at birth and L1–L2 in adults.
options: The cord does not shrink; it grows more slowly than the column.
Correct. Unequal growth leaves the cord ending higher in the canal.
The meninges do not pull the cord up; its end rises only because the column outgrows it.
Newborns have the same five lumbar vertebrae; it is the sacral vertebrae that fuse.

why.correct: The strip just in front of the central sulcus, the precentral gyrus, is the primary motor cortex. It sends commands to the skeletal muscles of the opposite side.
options: The primary somatosensory cortex is the strip just behind the central sulcus, in the parietal lobe.
The premotor cortex (motor association area) lies further forward, in front of the pinned strip.
Correct. The precentral gyrus is the primary motor cortex.
The prefrontal cortex is the front of the frontal lobe, well ahead of the motor strip.

why.correct: The area at the very back of the occipital lobe is the primary visual cortex, the first cortical area to receive visual signals.
options: Correct. The rearmost area of the occipital lobe is the primary visual cortex.
The primary auditory cortex is at the top of the temporal lobe, inside the lateral sulcus.
The visual association area surrounds the primary visual cortex, in front of the pinned area.
Wernicke's area is at the back of the upper temporal lobe, not at the back of the occipital lobe.

why.correct: Slow, effortful speech with good understanding is expressive (Broca's) aphasia, from damage to Broca's area in the lower left frontal lobe. Broca's area lies next to the motor cortex, so right-sided weakness often comes with it.
options: Correct. Broca's area is in the lower left frontal lobe.
Damage to Wernicke's area in the upper left temporal lobe causes fluent speech with poor understanding, the opposite pattern.
Right parietal damage typically causes neglect of the left side of space, not loss of speech.
Left occipital damage causes loss of vision in the right half of the scene, not trouble speaking.

why.correct: Fluent but meaningless speech, poor understanding and little awareness of the problem is receptive (Wernicke's) aphasia, from damage to Wernicke's area in the upper left temporal lobe.
options: Damage to Broca's area makes speech slow and effortful, while understanding stays mostly good.
Damage to the primary motor cortex weakens the muscles of the opposite side; it does not make speech meaningless.
Cerebellar damage makes speech slurred and poorly timed, but the words and their meaning are correct.
Correct. Wernicke's area is needed to understand language and choose meaningful words.

why.correct: Fluent speech means Broca's area works, and good understanding means Wernicke's area works. Repetition needs the word to travel from Wernicke's area to Broca's area, so a break in the connecting white matter causes conduction aphasia: poor repetition out of line with everything else.
options: Loss of both primary auditory cortices would stop the patient understanding speech, which this patient does well.
Damage to Broca's area makes spontaneous speech slow and effortful, not fluent.
Weak lip and tongue muscles slur all speech, not just repetition.
Correct. Damage to the connection between the two areas causes conduction aphasia.

why.correct: Each primary area has one job for one side of the body. Destroying the hand area of the left precentral gyrus weakens only the right hand; sensation, the other hand and language, handled by other areas, are unchanged.

variables.name: Strength of the right hand
variables.why: The left primary motor cortex sends commands to the muscles of the right side, and its hand area drives the right hand, so the right hand weakens.

variables.name: Strength of the left hand
variables.why: The left hand is controlled by the right hemisphere's motor cortex, which is undamaged.

variables.name: Ability to feel touch on the right hand
variables.why: Touch reaches the primary somatosensory cortex in the postcentral gyrus, behind the central sulcus, which was not damaged.

variables.name: Understanding of spoken words
variables.why: Understanding depends on Wernicke's area in the temporal lobe, far from the hand area of the motor strip.

why.correct: Adenosine builds up during waking and binds receptor proteins that inhibit arousal. Caffeine blocks those receptor proteins, so sleepiness falls and sleep is delayed, even though the adenosine is still there.

variables.name: Binding of adenosine to its receptor proteins in the brain
variables.why: Caffeine occupies the adenosine receptor proteins, so the adenosine that built up while you were awake cannot bind to them.

variables.name: Feeling of sleepiness
variables.why: Adenosine binding normally inhibits the brain's arousal systems. With binding blocked, that inhibition eases and you feel more alert.

variables.name: Time it takes to fall asleep once in bed
variables.why: With the sleep pressure signal blocked, the arousal systems stay active longer, so falling asleep takes longer.

why.correct: The cortex given to a body part depends on how densely it is supplied with sensory receptors, not on its size. The lips have many more per square centimeter than the back, and every incoming signal needs cortical neurons to receive it, so the lips get a large area.
options: Distance from the brain does not change signal strength; action potentials arrive at full size.
Correct. Sensory receptor density sets how much cortex a body part gets.
Touch from the back reaches the somatosensory cortex too; it simply needs less cortex because it has fewer sensory receptors.
The map in the somatosensory cortex is about sensation, and Broca's area does not receive touch signals.

why.correct: On the motor map the legs and feet lie on the medial surface, hanging into the longitudinal fissure. The right hemisphere controls the left side, so the left leg and foot weaken.
options: The hand area lies on the lateral surface, not the medial surface.
The right leg is controlled by the left hemisphere.
Correct. The medial right precentral gyrus controls the left leg and foot.
The face area lies lowest on the lateral surface, just above the lateral sulcus.

why.correct: The right parietal multimodal integration area attends to both sides of space. When it is damaged, the left side of space drops out of awareness even though the eyes and muscles work, so the person ignores everything on the left.
options: Loss of the right primary visual cortex would cause blindness in the left half of the scene, but his vision tests normal.
Broca's area is in the left frontal lobe and handles speech production.
His strength tests normal, and weakness would not explain ignoring the left half of his plate.
Correct. This is neglect of the left side of space after right parietal damage.

why.correct: She sees every feature, so the primary visual cortex works. Recognizing a face is the job of part of the visual association area; damage there leaves sight intact but removes recognition. She knows him by voice, so her memory of him is intact.
options: She can describe the features in detail, so she can see the face.
She knows him once he speaks, so she can understand and name him; the failure is visual only.
She recognizes his voice, so her memory of him is intact.
Correct. Seeing without recognizing points to the association area, not the primary area.

why.correct: The hippocampi are needed to form new declarative memories, so he has anterograde amnesia for facts and events. Procedural memory for skills uses the basal nuclei and cerebellum, so he can still improve at a practiced skill, as Henry Molaison did at mirror drawing.
options: This morning's meal is a new memory of an event, which needs the hippocampi to form.
New names are new facts, which need the hippocampi to form.
Correct. Procedural learning does not depend on the hippocampus.
A conversation an hour ago is a new memory of an event, which needs the hippocampi.

why.correct: This is retrograde amnesia. Memories from just before an injury are the least consolidated, so they are the most easily lost; older ones are already stored securely in the cortex.
options: Old memories are stored in the cortex and survive best; he kept his childhood memories.
Nothing suggests he lost skills; he lost memories of events.
Correct. Recent memories are lost first because they have not been consolidated.
The pattern is not random: it is the most recent memories that were lost.

why.correct: In REM sleep the EEG looks awake, the eyes dart, dreams are vivid, and brainstem neurons block the motor neurons to almost all skeletal muscles except the eye muscles and diaphragm. REM periods lengthen toward morning.
options: Yes. The REM EEG is fast and small, like being awake.
Yes. The body is limp except the eye muscles and the diaphragm, so breathing continues.
No. Slow, large delta waves are the sign of N3, deep non-REM sleep.
Yes. Most vivid, story-like dreams happen in REM sleep.
No. REM periods are shortest early in the night and grow longer toward morning.

why.correct: The line reaches N3 for long stretches in the first two cycles (about 0.6 to 1.2 and 2 to 2.6 hours), briefly around 4 hours, and not at all after that. Deep sleep is concentrated early in the night.
options: The graph shows N3 early and absent late, not evenly spread.
Correct. Nearly all N3 falls in the first three hours.
The last three hours contain REM and N2 but no N3.
Awakenings are at the top of the graph, the opposite of N3.

why.correct: REM periods on the graph grow from about 10 minutes early in the night to 40 minutes or more after 5 hours. Cutting the night at 4 hours removes the longest REM periods, while nearly all N3 has already happened.
options: Nearly all N3 falls in the first three hours, so a four-hour sleeper gets most of it.
N1 is brief at any time and is not concentrated late.
Correct. The longest REM periods come in the last part of the night.
N2 occurs in every cycle, including the first four hours.

why.correct: The EEG records the summed EPSPs and IPSPs of many aligned cortical neurons. In deep sleep huge numbers of them swing up and down together, so their currents add into slow, large waves. Awake, groups work on different things at different times, so the currents partly cancel into fast, small waves.
options: Correct. Synchrony makes the summed signal large.
The EEG mainly reflects synaptic potentials, not action potentials, and the size of the waves depends on how synchronized the neurons are.
The skull does not change thickness.
The EEG picks up the summed synaptic currents of the cortex, and muscles are most relaxed, not most active, during sleep.

why.correct: Touch from the left hand reaches the right hemisphere. With the corpus callosum cut, it cannot be passed to the left hemisphere, which produces speech in most people. So she cannot say "key," but the right hemisphere knows the object and guides the left hand to choose it.
options: Touch from one hand reaches mainly the opposite hemisphere, and without the corpus callosum it cannot be shared.
Correct. The right hemisphere knows the key but cannot speak it.
Sensation in the left hand is normal; it reaches the right hemisphere, which can guide the hand.
Naming needs the left hemisphere, which produces speech in most people, and the touch cannot reach it; the right hemisphere can still guide the left hand.

why.correct: Sound reaches the primary auditory cortex, Wernicke's area recognizes the word, a curved band of white matter carries it to Broca's area, Broca's area plans the speech, and the face area of the primary motor cortex drives the muscles.
options: Hearing starts in the primary auditory cortex of the temporal lobe.
Wernicke's area, beside it, recognizes the word and its meaning.
The arcuate fasciculus links the temporal and frontal language areas.
Broca's area assembles fluent speech.
The motor cortex's face area moves the lips, tongue and throat.

why.correct: Faces are recognized by the visual association area around and below the primary visual cortex, not by the primary auditory cortex, which receives sound.
options: Right. Visual signals relay in the thalamus on their way to the cortex.
Right. The primary visual cortex is the first cortical stop.
This is the error. The visual association area recognizes faces; the primary auditory cortex receives sound.
Right. Integration areas combine what you see with other senses and memory.

why.correct: Impulsiveness, poor judgment and trouble planning with normal movement, speech and memory are loss of executive function, run by the prefrontal cortex at the front of the frontal lobes, as in the case of Phineas Gage.
options: Primary motor cortex damage causes weakness, and his movement is normal.
Correct. The prefrontal cortex runs executive function.
Primary somatosensory damage causes numbness, not changes in behavior.
Hippocampal damage stops new memories forming, and his memory is normal.

why.correct: When people are prevented from rehearsing or grouping, working memory holds about four chunks. Many exams still give the older figure of 7 plus or minus 2.
options: People can hold more than one item; you can keep a short list in mind.
Twenty items is far beyond what people hold without rehearsal.
Correct. About four chunks.
Long-term memory has no known limit, but working memory is small.

why.correct: Strong, repeated activity lets calcium into the postsynaptic cell, which triggers the insertion of more glutamate receptor proteins. The same glutamate now opens more channels, giving a larger EPSP.
options: A more negative resting potential would move the cell further from threshold. That is not what long-term potentiation changes; the EPSP grows because more glutamate receptor proteins open.
Myelin speeds conduction along an axon; it does not change the size of an EPSP at a synapse on the dendrites.
Fewer receptor proteins would shrink the EPSP.
Correct. More receptor proteins mean a bigger response to the same transmitter.
